---
title: "Images and image stacks"
subtitle: "Microscopy stacks, movies and photographs on a figure: the pixels stay as measured, everything you change is a view"
---

A **fluximg** is one scientific image saved together with what is known about it: its pixels in
any number of dimensions (channels, depth, time, or a dimension of your own such as trial), the
physical size of a pixel, the name and colour of each channel, and layers drawn on the same pixel
grid (another image, segmented objects with a table, lines and circles). It is the image
counterpart of a [semantic plot](semantic-plots.qmd).

Flux stores the pixels once and never changes them. What you adjust (the plane you look at,
contrast, colours, a projection, the region shown, a scale bar) is a **view**: a handful of
numbers kept on the placed image. Two placements of one image can show different planes and
contrast, an agent can read and set the same numbers, and you can always go back to the pixels
as they were measured.

# Saving an image from Python

A fluximg is written by [fluxplot](https://github.com/fluxsci/fluxplot) (writing needs a zstd
library: install the `fluxplot[images]` extra; Python 3.14 has one built in). It is a folder,
`<name>.fluximg`, saved into your project's `plots/` folder like any plot.

A confocal z-stack, two channels:

```python
import fluxplot as fp

# stack: shape (2, 31, 1024, 1024) = channel, z, y, x
fp.imsave("plots/neuron_stack", stack, dims=("c", "z", "y", "x"),
          pixel_size=0.1, unit="µm", coords={"z": z_positions_um},
          channels=[{"name": "membrane", "color": "#ff00ff"},
                    {"name": "nuclei", "color": "#00ffff"}],
          recipe=True)
```

A two-photon time-lapse, with the segmented cells and their table as a layer:

```python
img = fp.fluximg(movie, dims=("t", "c", "y", "x"), dt=0.5, pixel_size=0.4,
                 channels=["GCaMP", "tdTomato"])
img.add_labels("cells", cell_labels, table=cells, key="cell_id")   # one row per cell
img.add_shapes("tracks", lines=track_paths, key="track_id")
img.save("plots/timelapse", recipe=True)
```

A plain 2-D image needs no `dims`, and an RGB photograph is marked as one:

```python
fp.imsave("plots/field", field_image, pixel_size=0.65)
fp.imsave("plots/specimen", photo, photometric="rgb")
```

`recipe=True` writes `<name>.recipe.json` beside the folder, so the image can be made again.
`save` prints what it wrote and why.

**How pixels are stored.** Integer data (8-, 16- or 32-bit) is always stored exactly. Float data
is stored **compactly** (16-bit steps across each channel's own range; Flux shows it as "compact
16-bit") when that is provably harmless: one step must be smaller than a tenth of the typical
difference between neighbouring pixels, in every channel. Any real noisy image passes. When an
image fails that test (a constant or piecewise-constant image, or a range stretched by a few
extreme values), the writer keeps the floats exactly and its report says why. Pass
`lossless=True` to keep floats exactly in every case. Large planes (over 1024 px on a side) are
stored as tiles with smaller overview copies, so Flux can show them at once.

# Putting it on a figure

Image bundles appear in the **Plots** rail and the **Plot gallery** as one tile each, marked
**▦** ("image stack"), with a picture and a line such as "2 channels · 31 z · 1,024 × 1,024 ·
uint16". Double-click a tile, press **Enter**, or drag it onto a figure. You can also use
**Import** (**Ctrl+Shift+K**) and choose the `fluximg.json` file inside the `.fluximg` folder (a
file dialog cannot pick a folder), or drag the `.fluximg` folder in from your file manager.

- Images need a saved Flux project. In an unsaved or older standalone figure, Flux says so
  before copying anything.
- Flux copies the folder into the project once (a copy-on-write clone where the file system
  offers one, so even a large stack takes a fraction of a second). Placing the same image again,
  however many times, shows the same copy.
- An image has no printed size of its own: it lands at one image pixel per canvas pixel, scaled
  down to the figure's width when it would be wider.
- **It follows its source.** While the project is open, re-running the script that wrote the
  folder replaces every placed copy with the new version. Each keeps its view and crop where
  they still fit; if something had to change (fewer planes, a channel gone), a notice says what.
  One **Ctrl+Z** brings back the previous version.

# The live view

Select an image and press **R**, or double-click it. The image stays where it is and becomes
live: a pink frame marks it, and its **control board** stands round it on the canvas. There is
no menu to open. Everything the image can show is on the board at once, and each thing answers
the pointer where it is.

- The **console** stands at one side: the image's name, one **strip** per channel (its histogram
  is its contrast control), a row of **paper keys**, and a small map once the frame is zoomed in.
- **Depth** stands at the other side like a y axis, and **time** (or any other dimension) lies
  under the image like an x axis. Each is a **rail**: a plot of the stack that you scrub.
- **Layers**, when the image has any, are a card beside the board.

A wide, low image (a line-scan movie) takes its console under it instead, where the room is. Near
an edge of the canvas the instruments change sides, and only when the image fills the window do
they stand over its edges: zoom the canvas out (**Ctrl** + wheel) to give them room. No
instrument ever covers another.

Rest the pointer on anything on the board and a small label names it and its key. **R** again,
the **×** on the console, or a click elsewhere on the canvas closes the view. **Escape** lets go
of one thing at a time: an open chooser, a movie that is playing, whatever is in hand, then the
view. Placing the first image of a session shows a message saying how to open the live view.

Every gesture is **one undo step**: a drag, a typed value, or a run of wheel notches (it ends
after a short pause). **Ctrl+Z** works while the view is open. Keys with **Ctrl** keep their
usual meaning; plain keys belong to the board, and they are the same wherever the pointer is.
**F** opens the usual property menu.

## What the pointer reads

Over the image, the console's head says where the pointer is in the image's own units, every
channel's strip marks that pixel's value on its histogram, and four small ticks on the frame ride
along with the pointer. Over an object of a layer, the object lights up, and a card beside the
pointer names it, its layer and the first columns of its table. Off the image, the head says what
the image is: its planes, its size in pixels and the size of a pixel.

## In hand

The wheel over the image, and a drag on it, drive whatever the view has **in hand**; that thing
is outlined pink on the board. The view opens holding its first rail by itself, so the wheel over
the image steps planes at once while it still pans the canvas everywhere else. Take something in
hand with its key and the wheel drives it from anywhere on screen:

| Key | In hand | The wheel | A drag on the image |
|---|---|---|---|
| **t**, **z** | that rail (other dimensions get **q** or **`**) | steps planes; down is the next one | moves the image under its frame, when zoomed in |
| **1**–**6** | that channel: its white point, then (pressed again) its black point, then gamma | moves the point | pulls its contrast |
| **v** | the frame | zooms on the spot under the pointer | moves the image under the frame |
| **x** | the inset tool | | draws the inset's box |

Working an instrument with the mouse (dragging a handle, scrubbing a rail, rolling the wheel
over a strip) never takes it in hand: afterwards the wheel over the image still steps planes.
**Shift** makes a wheel notch ten times larger, **Alt** ten times finer.

## Moving through a stack

A rail's well plots each shown channel's mean signal per plane, so you can see where to go
before you go there. The pink line is the plane on screen, a dot rides each channel's trace on
it, and a paper flag beside it says the plane's number and where that is ("13 · 12 µm"). The
scale is in the axis' own unit, at round values.

- **Wheel** over the image or over the rail steps planes. **← / →** step along the rail under the
  image, **↑ / ↓** through depth (**Shift**: ten).
- **Drag** along a rail to scrub. Resting on it names the plane under the pointer.
- The round **play** key, or **Space**, plays: at the real frame rate when the dimension is time
  in seconds, otherwise 12 planes a second. Its ring fills as the stack goes by. The small dial
  beside it is the **speed** (¼× to 4×): click it or roll the wheel over it.
- A stack shows the right plane at once while you move, and sharpens a moment later. The lamp
  beside the image's name is solid when the picture on screen is final, hollow while a sharper
  one is on its way.

**Projections.** Press **e**, or the key at the rail's far end, and pick a statistic (max, mean,
min, sum, std; **1**–**6**, or the arrows and **Enter**). It starts over the whole dimension,
the usual maximum projection of a stack. The run is a pink band on the rail with a grip at each
end: drag a grip to resize it, drag inside to slide it, or **Shift**-drag on a rail to draw a new
one. The wheel over the band widens or narrows the run around its middle; over the rest of the
rail, or over the image, it slides the run. (Picked by its number, the run is in hand: the wheel
sizes it from anywhere until **Escape**.) Choosing **off** returns to the plane in the middle of
the run.

## Contrast and colour

Each channel's strip is a lamp in the channel's colour with its digit, the channel's name, its
window in numbers, and its histogram. The histogram is of the **pixels on screen** (the plane or
projection, inside the frame), drawn in the channel's own colours between its black and white
points, so it changes as you move through the stack; the whole image's histogram is the faint
outline behind it.

- **Drag a pink handle** to move the black or white point; **drag between them** to slide the
  window. The **wheel** over the plot moves the nearer point.
- **Double-click** the plot for Auto on that channel. Click one of the two numbers to type a
  value (**Enter** keeps it, **Escape** drops it).
- The **lamp** is the switch: click it to hide or show the channel (**Shift** + its digit).
  **Alt**-click it, or **Alt** + its digit, to see that channel alone.
- With the pointer on a strip, its own keys come out: **Auto**, the **curve** (linear, log,
  gamma), **Colour** (a drawer of swatches: gray, green, magenta, cyan, yellow, red, blue,
  viridis, magma; with Invert and a key that puts the channel back to how the image came), and
  **Only this channel**. The paper line across the plot is the transfer curve: pull the dot at
  its middle up or down to bend it (gamma).
- While you work a strip, the plot says what share of the channel's values the window clips at
  each end ("1.4 %"), estimated from the whole image's histogram.

Press a channel's digit to take it **in hand**: the wheel then moves its white point from
anywhere, and **dragging on the image** pulls its contrast (right narrows the window about its
centre, left widens it; up and down slide it brighter and darker). The window never leaves the
channel's own range of values.

**Auto** (**a**, or the first paper key) sets every channel's window from the pixels in view;
with a channel in hand it sets that channel's alone. Rest the pointer on the key and each strip
shows, dashed, where its two points would go. Each press moves to the next window on a ladder:
0.1–99.9 %, 1–99.8 %, 1–99 % of those pixels, then their full range, and round again. The
Inspector's Auto uses the percentiles the whole image carries instead, so it gives the same
window on every plane.

**Split channels** (**s**) makes one panel per channel, each alone in gray with its name. Rest
the pointer on the key and the figure shows, dashed, where each panel would go: to the image's
right, each the image's size, when the figure has room; otherwise the image and its channels
share the image's own box as a grid, the image first (a figure clips what lies outside it, so
panels past its edge could not be seen). Nothing else on the figure moves.

## The paper keys

| Key | Paper key | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| **a** | Auto contrast | Every channel's window from the pixels in view (the channel in hand, when there is one) |
| **s** | Split channels | One panel per channel |
| **v** | Frame | The frame in hand: wheel to zoom, drag to move. **Shift+V**: the whole image again |
| **x** | Inset | Then drag a box on the image |
| **b** | Scale bar | It needs a pixel size; without one, pressing it tells you so |
| **w** | Position stamp | Where along depth or time the picture is |
| **c** | Channel names | Each in its channel's colour |
| **g** | Calibration bar | Each shown channel's colours from its black point to its white point, with both values |

A key that is on is lit. The four annotations are drawn as vectors on the image, and each one
that is shown is a thing you can take hold of on the picture:

- **Drag it to another corner**: the four corners are marked while you carry it. **Shift** with
  its key (or a Shift-click on its paper key) sends it to the next corner too.
- **Roll the wheel over the scale bar** to step its length through round values (1, 2, 5, 10 …);
  back at the length the picture picks by itself, nothing is stored.
- **Roll the wheel over the stamp, the channel names or the calibration bar** to change its text
  size, half a point a notch.

The Inspector has the same settings as numbers, with the bar's thickness and colours.

## Layers and objects

The layers card lists each layer, top of the stack first: a lamp in its colour (click: show or
hide), its name, and how many objects it holds. Click a layer of objects to open it: its objects
by name, with the first columns of their table. Resting on an object's row lights it on the
image, and resting on an object on the image lights its row. On a layer's row, the small **%**
is its opacity (roll the wheel over it, or drag it sideways), and two small keys switch its
object names on the image and open its colours. Type in the field at the top to filter by name
or value. Long lists show the first 300 objects of a layer; filter to find the rest.

Press **d** to give the card the keyboard; it is outlined pink while it has it, and **Escape**
gives the keys back to the board. Working the card with the mouse never takes the keyboard.

| Key | Action |
|---|---|
| **↑ / ↓** | Walk the list (**Shift**: move the layer up or down the stack) |
| **→ / ←** | Open or close a layer's objects |
| **x** | Show or hide the layer |
| **e** | Its opacity in hand, for the wheel |
| **c** | Its colours |
| **q** | Object names on the image |
| **a** | The filter |

## The frame and insets

The frame is a window onto the whole image: the box stays where it is on the figure. Press
**v** to take it in hand (the corners of the pink frame thicken into handles): the wheel over the
image zooms in on the spot under the pointer, and a drag moves the image under the frame. Once
the frame shows only part of the image, a drag on the image moves it whether or not the frame is
in hand.

While the frame is zoomed in (or in hand), the console shows a **map**: the whole image, small,
with the frame's rectangle on it and the regions already pulled out as insets dashed. Drag the
rectangle, or press anywhere on the map, to move the frame there; the wheel over the map zooms.
Beside it are how far in the frame is ("2.5×"), how many pixels it shows, and two keys: **true
pixels** or smoothed ones when the image is magnified (**n**), and **Whole image** (**Shift+V**),
which shows all of the image again in the box it has.

**x** takes the **inset** tool in hand: drag a box on the image, and on release it becomes a new
panel showing that region with a scale bar, while the image outlines the region and keeps its
own frame. With the frame zoomed in, press **x** twice instead to pull out the frame as it is;
the image then shows the whole of itself again.

The region's rectangle on the image stays a handle: **drag its edge** and the region moves, the
inset showing what is under it as you go; **roll the wheel over its edge** and the region gets
smaller or larger about its middle (the inset shows it closer or wider). Inside the rectangle the
image is still the image's.

An inset goes beside the image when the figure has room: to the right at the image's height,
else below it, no wider than the image. Otherwise it stands on the image, in its top-right
corner at two fifths of its height, and the live view closes with the inset selected so you can
drag it where you want. A message says where it went.

## Linked panels

Panels made by **Split channels** or pulled out as an inset stay linked to the image they came
from: move one to another plane, change its projection, or drag a channel's black or white
point, and the others follow. What each panel shows stays its own (which channels, their
colours, its frame, its annotations). The Inspector says how many panels a panel moves with,
and **Unlink** sets it free.

# The Inspector

With an image selected, the Inspector shows the same settings as numbers, whether or not the
live view is open: **Image** (what it is, the pixel size, how it is stored, where it came from,
and a **Live view** button), **Channels** (Blend or Single, each channel's colour or colour map,
scale, black, white and gamma, with **Auto**), **Position** (the plane along each dimension, a
projection and its run), **Layers**, **Annotations** (scale bar length, thickness, text size,
corner and colour; the stamp, channel names, calibration bar and object names) and **View**
(true or smoothed pixels, background or transparent, and the region shown in image pixels).
Setting a value back to its default removes it from the stored view.

# What exports contain

Exports (SVG, PNG, TIFF, PDF), figures in [Paper](../modes/paper.qmd) and headless renders
(`flux render-figure`) draw each image's picture from the full-resolution pixels at the output's
own resolution: 300 dpi at the image's printed size for SVG, PDF and Paper, the export's own
resolution for PNG and TIFF, at most 4096 × 4096 pixels per image. Every output pixel is drawn, so no viewer can
blur a magnified image. Layers of objects and shapes, object names, the scale bar, stamps and
labels stay vectors. The picture on the canvas and the export come from one renderer, so they
show the same pixels.

# Limits of this first version

- Images go on **figures** only. A slide refuses them for now ("keep them in a figure").
- Only `.fluximg` folders can be placed. TIFF and other microscope files cannot be dragged in
  yet: save them with fluxplot first.
- There is no 3-D rendering. Depth is a dimension to step through or project.
- Images are placed from the project's `plots/` folder; the global plot library does not list
  them.
- The live view reads whole planes at the resolution it needs. A very large mosaic zoomed in to
  its own pixels is read whole, not tile by tile.
- The live view shows at most six channels and three image layers at once; the picture at rest
  and exports show them all.
